decks.title: Analytical Chemistry — Part 1: Colours, sodium hydroxide and ammonium salts
goals: State the colours of common salts of copper, iron, zinc and lead and of their solutions
Predict the precipitate formed when sodium hydroxide is added to a salt solution, and what excess alkali does
Write balanced equations for the precipitation reactions
Describe how warming with sodium hydroxide shows that a salt is an ammonium salt

slides.heading: Detective work with test tubes
slides.body_md: Part 1 — **Analytical chemistry** finds out what a substance is made of. In **qualitative analysis** we identify the ions in a salt from simple observations: its **colour**, and the **precipitate** it gives with an alkali.

rows: Colour of the solid or solution
Narrows down the metal (blue often means copper)
Whether the precipitate dissolves in excess alkali
A gas given off on warming with alkali

visual.alt: Table of four clues used in qualitative analysis and what each tells us

slides.narration: Namaste! A chemist handed an unlabelled bottle behaves like a detective. Simple clues, such as the colour of a salt and the colour of the solid that forms when an alkali is added, tell us which metal ion is present. In this part we learn the colours of common salts, the action of sodium hydroxide on their solutions, and a quick test for ammonium salts.

slides.heading: Colours of salts and their solutions
slides.body_md: Salts of **sodium, potassium, calcium, zinc, lead and ammonium** are **white** solids and give **colourless** solutions. Salts of some **transition metals** are coloured, and the colour of the solid often differs from that of the solution.

visual.alt: Table of the colours of common salts as solids and in solution

slides.narration: Start with colour. Salts of sodium, potassium, calcium, zinc, lead and ammonium are white, and their solutions are colourless. Copper salts are usually blue or green. Iron two salts are pale green, while iron three salts are yellowish brown. So a pale green solution hints at iron two ions, and a blue one at copper. Colour alone is only a hint, so we confirm it with an alkali.

slides.heading: Coloured oxides and other compounds
slides.body_md: Some insoluble compounds have colours worth remembering, because they appear as **residues** and **precipitates** in many reactions.

rows: White when cold, yellow when hot

visual.alt: Table of the colours of oxides and carbonates of copper, zinc, lead and iron

slides.narration: A few insoluble compounds turn up again and again. Copper oxide is black and copper carbonate is green. Zinc oxide is white when cold but yellow when hot. Lead two oxide is yellow, red lead is bright red, and lead four oxide is dark brown. Iron three oxide is reddish brown, the colour of rust.

slides.heading: Quick check: colour of a solution
slides.body_md: Use the colour of a salt solution to name the ion it hints at.
slides.narration: Quick check. Remember which iron ion gives a pale green solution and which gives a yellowish brown one.

slides.heading: Sodium hydroxide, a few drops at a time
slides.body_md: Sodium hydroxide gives **hydroxide ions**. Most metal hydroxides are **insoluble**, so they appear as **precipitates**, each with its own colour. Add the alkali **drop by drop**, then **in excess**, and note both observations.

slides.narration: Sodium hydroxide solution supplies hydroxide ions. Most metal hydroxides do not dissolve in water, so a solid called a precipitate appears. Iron two ions give a dirty green precipitate, iron three ions a reddish brown one, copper ions a pale blue one, and zinc and lead ions white ones. Then keep adding alkali: the zinc and lead precipitates dissolve, but the others stay.

slides.heading: Equations for the coloured precipitates
slides.body_md: The metal hydroxide precipitates; the sodium salt stays in solution. These precipitates do **not** dissolve in excess sodium hydroxide.

visual.alt: Table of equations for sodium hydroxide with iron(II), iron(III), copper(II) and calcium salts and the precipitate colours

slides.narration: Here are the equations. In each one, the metal hydroxide comes out as a precipitate and a sodium salt stays dissolved. Iron two sulphate gives dirty green iron two hydroxide, iron three chloride gives reddish brown iron three hydroxide, and copper sulphate gives pale blue copper hydroxide. Calcium nitrate gives a white precipitate. None of these dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide.

slides.heading: Worked example: iron(II) or iron(III)?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Two bottles, P and Q, hold iron salt solutions. With sodium hydroxide, P gives a **dirty green** precipitate and Q a **reddish-brown** one. Identify the ion in each and write the equation for Q, taking Q as iron(III) sulphate.

**Step 1.** Dirty green → iron(II) hydroxide → **P has Fe²⁺**.

**Step 2.** Reddish brown → iron(III) hydroxide → **Q has Fe³⁺**.

**Step 3.** Fe₂(SO₄)₃ + 6NaOH → 2Fe(OH)₃ + 3Na₂SO₄.

**Note.** The dirty green solid slowly turns brown at its surface in air, as iron(II) is oxidised to iron(III).

visual.alt: Table identifying the iron ions in bottles P and Q from the colour of the precipitate

slides.narration: The colour of the precipitate decides it. A dirty green precipitate is iron two hydroxide, so bottle P contains iron two ions. A reddish brown precipitate is iron three hydroxide, so bottle Q contains iron three ions. For iron three sulphate, one unit needs six units of sodium hydroxide. Notice too that the green solid browns slowly in air as it is oxidised.

slides.heading: Quick check: a coloured precipitate
slides.body_md: Predict the precipitate from a pale green solution.
slides.narration: Quick check. Match the precipitate to the iron ion, and think about whether it dissolves in excess.

slides.heading: Zinc and lead: precipitates that dissolve
slides.body_md: Zinc and lead salts give **white** precipitates that **dissolve in excess** sodium hydroxide, forming soluble **sodium zincate** and **sodium plumbite**. Zinc and lead hydroxides are **amphoteric**: they react with an alkali as well as with an acid.

visual.alt: Table of equations for zinc sulphate and lead nitrate with a little and with excess sodium hydroxide

slides.narration: Zinc and lead behave differently. A few drops of sodium hydroxide give a white precipitate, gelatinous for zinc and chalky for lead. But add more alkali and the precipitate disappears, leaving a clear, colourless solution of sodium zincate or sodium plumbite. That happens because zinc and lead hydroxides react with alkalis as well as acids.

slides.heading: Worked example: how much alkali?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** What mass of sodium hydroxide is just enough to precipitate all the copper from a solution of 31.9 g of copper(II) sulphate? (Cu = 63.5, S = 32, O = 16, Na = 23, H = 1)

**Step 1.** CuSO₄ + 2NaOH → Cu(OH)₂ + Na₂SO₄: 1 mole CuSO₄ needs 2 moles NaOH.

**Step 2.** CuSO₄ = 63.5 + 32 + 64 = 159.5; moles = 31.9 ÷ 159.5 = 0.2.

**Step 3.** NaOH = 2 × 0.2 = 0.4 mole; mass = 0.4 × 40 = **16 g**.

visual.alt: Table of the steps from 31.9 grams of copper sulphate to 16 grams of sodium hydroxide

slides.narration: From the equation, each unit of copper sulphate needs two units of sodium hydroxide. The molar mass of copper sulphate is one hundred fifty nine point five, so thirty one point nine grams is zero point two mole. Twice that is zero point four mole of sodium hydroxide, and since its molar mass is forty, the mass needed is sixteen grams.

slides.heading: Sodium hydroxide and ammonium salts
slides.body_md: An **ammonium salt** warmed with sodium hydroxide gives **ammonia**. The stronger base drives out the weaker one. Identify the gas by its **pungent smell**, by **moist red litmus turning blue**, and by **dense white fumes** with a rod dipped in concentrated hydrochloric acid.

visual.alt: Equation: ammonium chloride plus sodium hydroxide gives sodium chloride, water and ammonia
visual.caption: Warming an ammonium salt with sodium hydroxide

slides.narration: Ammonium salts are white and dissolve to give colourless solutions, so colour does not help. Instead, warm the salt with sodium hydroxide. Ammonia gas is given off, with a sharp smell. It turns moist red litmus paper blue, and it gives dense white fumes of ammonium chloride with a glass rod dipped in concentrated hydrochloric acid.

slides.heading: Worked example: is it an ammonium salt?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** White crystals R are warmed with sodium hydroxide solution. A gas turns moist red litmus blue. With barium chloride solution, a solution of R gives a white precipitate insoluble in dilute HCl. Identify R and write the equation for the warming.

**Step 1.** Alkaline gas on warming with NaOH → **ammonium ion**.

**Step 2.** White precipitate with barium chloride, insoluble in acid → **sulphate ion**.

**Step 3.** R is **ammonium sulphate**: (NH₄)₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O + 2NH₃.

nodes.label: Gas turns moist red litmus blue?

visual.alt: Flow for testing whether a white salt is an ammonium salt by warming it with sodium hydroxide

slides.narration: Take the clues one at a time. A gas that turns moist red litmus blue, given off on warming with sodium hydroxide, can only be ammonia, so the salt contains ammonium ions. A white precipitate with barium chloride that does not dissolve in acid shows sulphate ions. Together they point to ammonium sulphate.

slides.body_md: Decide what an alkaline gas on warming with sodium hydroxide tells you.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Salts of Na, K, Ca, Zn, Pb and NH₄⁺ are white with colourless solutions; copper salts are blue or green; iron(II) pale green; iron(III) yellowish brown.
NaOH, a few drops: Fe²⁺ dirty green, Fe³⁺ reddish brown, Cu²⁺ pale blue, Zn²⁺ and Pb²⁺ white precipitates.
In excess NaOH, only the zinc and lead hydroxides dissolve (sodium zincate, sodium plumbite).
Ammonium salts warmed with NaOH give ammonia: moist red litmus turns blue.

visual.alt: Summary table of the action of sodium hydroxide, a few drops and in excess, on six cations

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. The colour of a salt gives a first hint. Sodium hydroxide then gives a dirty green precipitate with iron two, reddish brown with iron three, pale blue with copper, and white with zinc, lead and calcium. Only the zinc and lead precipitates dissolve in excess. Ammonium salts give ammonia when warmed with the alkali.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Always state two observations: the precipitate with a few drops, then its behaviour in excess.
Give the colour and the nature of the precipitate (gelatinous, chalky) where you can.
Write formulae of hydroxides carefully: Fe(OH)₂, Fe(OH)₃, Cu(OH)₂, Zn(OH)₂, Pb(OH)₂.
For an ammonium salt, the word “warm” and the litmus test both earn marks.

rows: Fe(OH)₂ is dirty green; Fe(OH)₃ is reddish brown
It does not; it dissolves in excess NH₄OH
Ammonia is given off on warming

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 1 and their fixes

slides.narration: Some tips. Examiners want two observations, one with a few drops of alkali and one with excess. Describe the precipitate fully, with its colour and whether it is gelatinous or chalky. Check your hydroxide formulae, and do not mix up the two iron hydroxides. For ammonium salts, mention warming and the moist red litmus test.

decks.title: Analytical Chemistry — Part 2: Ammonium hydroxide and amphoteric substances
goals: Describe what a little and then excess ammonium hydroxide does to solutions of iron, copper, zinc and lead salts
Choose a reagent to distinguish between two salt solutions and state the observations
Define an amphoteric substance with examples
Write equations for sodium hydroxide with aluminium, zinc and lead and with their oxides and hydroxides

slides.heading: A weaker alkali, new clues
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **Ammonium hydroxide** (aqueous ammonia) is a **weak alkali**. It precipitates the same hydroxides, but in **excess** it behaves differently from sodium hydroxide, giving us a second test.

visual.alt: Table comparing sodium hydroxide and ammonium hydroxide and which precipitates each dissolves in excess

slides.narration: Ammonium hydroxide, a solution of ammonia in water, is a weak alkali. With a few drops it gives much the same hydroxide precipitates as sodium hydroxide. The difference shows up in excess. Sodium hydroxide dissolves the zinc and lead precipitates, but ammonium hydroxide dissolves the zinc and copper ones. Using both reagents, we can tell apart cations that look alike.

slides.heading: Ammonium hydroxide, a few drops
slides.body_md: A few drops of ammonium hydroxide give the **same coloured precipitates** as sodium hydroxide; the ammonium salt stays in solution.

visual.alt: Table of equations for a few drops of ammonium hydroxide with five salt solutions

slides.narration: With just a few drops of ammonium hydroxide, the results look familiar. Iron two gives a dirty green precipitate, iron three a reddish brown one, lead and zinc give white ones, and copper gives pale blue. The equations are like those for sodium hydroxide, except that an ammonium salt, not a sodium salt, is left in solution.

slides.heading: Excess ammonium hydroxide: copper and zinc
slides.body_md:
In excess, ammonium hydroxide **dissolves** two precipitates by forming soluble **complex salts**:

- **Copper(II) hydroxide** → a **deep (inky) blue** solution of tetraamminecopper(II) sulphate, [Cu(NH₃)₄]SO₄.
- **Zinc hydroxide** → a **colourless** solution of tetraamminezinc(II) sulphate, [Zn(NH₃)₄]SO₄.

Iron(II), iron(III) and **lead** hydroxides do **not** dissolve.

slides.narration: Now add ammonium hydroxide in excess. The pale blue copper precipitate dissolves to give a deep, inky blue solution, which is a very sensitive sign of copper ions. The white zinc precipitate also dissolves, leaving a colourless solution. Both form soluble complex salts with ammonia. The iron and lead precipitates stay put.

slides.body_md: The ammonium salt formed in the first step takes part in dissolving the precipitate. The two complex-forming equations have the same shape.

slides.narration: Here is what happens in excess. Copper hydroxide reacts with ammonium sulphate and more ammonium hydroxide to give tetraammine copper two sulphate and water, which is deep blue. Zinc hydroxide reacts in exactly the same pattern to give a colourless complex salt. Lead and iron hydroxides do not react, so their precipitates remain.

slides.heading: Worked example: telling pairs apart
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Suggest a reagent to distinguish each pair, and state the observation for each solution: (a) zinc nitrate and lead nitrate; (b) iron(II) sulphate and iron(III) sulphate; (c) ammonium chloride and sodium chloride.

**(a)** Excess **NH₄OH**: zinc — white precipitate **dissolves**; lead — white precipitate **stays**.

**(b)** **NaOH**: iron(II) — **dirty green**; iron(III) — **reddish brown**.

**(c)** **NaOH, warm**: ammonium chloride — **ammonia** turns moist red litmus blue; sodium chloride — **no gas**.

The two iron salts differ in the colour of their precipitates. And only the ammonium salt gives off ammonia when warmed with sodium hydroxide.

slides.heading: Identifying a cation: a flow
slides.body_md: Combine the clues in order: **colour of the precipitate** with a few drops, then its behaviour in **excess NaOH** and in **excess NH₄OH**.

nodes.label: Add a few drops of NaOH
Dirty green: Fe²⁺; reddish brown: Fe³⁺; pale blue: Cu²⁺
Yes: add excess NH₄OH to a fresh sample

visual.alt: Flow chart for identifying iron(II), iron(III), copper, calcium, zinc and lead ions using sodium hydroxide and ammonium hydroxide

slides.narration: Here is a simple plan. Add a few drops of sodium hydroxide. A coloured precipitate names the ion at once: dirty green for iron two, reddish brown for iron three, pale blue for copper. If the precipitate is white, add excess sodium hydroxide. If it stays, the ion is calcium. If it dissolves, test a fresh sample with excess aqueous ammonia: zinc dissolves, lead does not.

slides.heading: Amphoteric substances
slides.body_md: An **amphoteric** substance reacts with **both acids and bases** to form a salt and water. The **oxides and hydroxides of aluminium, zinc and lead** are amphoteric, and the **metals** themselves react with hot, concentrated caustic alkalis (NaOH, KOH) to give **hydrogen**.

visual.alt: Table of zinc oxide, lead(II) oxide and aluminium oxide reacting with an acid and with sodium hydroxide

slides.narration: Some oxides cannot make up their minds. Zinc oxide, lead two oxide and aluminium oxide react with acids, like a base, and with sodium hydroxide, like an acid, giving a salt and water each time. Such substances are called amphoteric. Their hydroxides are amphoteric too, which is why zinc and lead hydroxides dissolve in excess sodium hydroxide.

slides.heading: Metals that react with alkalis
slides.body_md:
Aluminium, zinc and lead react with **hot, concentrated** sodium hydroxide to give a salt and **hydrogen**. Aluminium also needs water:

- 2Al + 2NaOH + 2H₂O → 2NaAlO₂ + 3H₂ (sodium aluminate)
- Zn + 2NaOH → Na₂ZnO₂ + H₂ (sodium zincate)
- Pb + 2NaOH → Na₂PbO₂ + H₂ (sodium plumbite)

visual.alt: Equation: two aluminium plus two sodium hydroxide plus two water gives two sodium aluminate plus three hydrogen
visual.caption: Aluminium with hot sodium hydroxide solution

slides.narration: The metals themselves react with hot, concentrated caustic soda. Aluminium, together with water, gives sodium aluminate and hydrogen. Zinc gives sodium zincate and hydrogen, and lead gives sodium plumbite and hydrogen. The gas burns with a pop. This is why aluminium vessels should not be scrubbed with strong washing soda or caustic soda.

slides.heading: Worked example: hydrogen from aluminium
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** 2.7 g of aluminium foil dissolves completely in hot sodium hydroxide solution. Find the volume of hydrogen at STP. (Al = 27; molar volume 22.4 L)

**Step 1.** 2Al + 2NaOH + 2H₂O → 2NaAlO₂ + 3H₂: 2 moles Al give 3 moles H₂.

**Step 2.** Moles of Al = 2.7 ÷ 27 = 0.1.

**Step 3.** Moles of H₂ = 0.1 × 3 ÷ 2 = 0.15; volume = 0.15 × 22.4 = **3.36 L**.

visual.alt: Table of the steps from 2.7 grams of aluminium to 3.36 litres of hydrogen

slides.narration: The equation shows that two units of aluminium give three units of hydrogen. Two point seven grams of aluminium is zero point one mole, since its molar mass is twenty seven. That gives one and a half times as much hydrogen, zero point one five mole, which occupies zero point one five times twenty two point four, or three point three six litres, at standard conditions.

slides.heading: Hydroxides with caustic alkali
slides.body_md: The amphoteric **hydroxides** dissolve in sodium hydroxide; this is what happens when the zinc or lead precipitate disappears in excess alkali.

visual.alt: Table of aluminium, zinc and lead hydroxides reacting with sodium hydroxide and the salts formed

slides.narration: The hydroxides follow the same pattern as the oxides. Aluminium hydroxide gives sodium aluminate, zinc hydroxide gives sodium zincate, and lead hydroxide gives sodium plumbite, with water in each case. With potassium hydroxide the salts are potassium aluminate, potassium zincate and potassium plumbite.

Aqueous ammonia gives the same precipitates as caustic soda at first, but in excess it dissolves the copper precipitate to a deep blue solution and the zinc precipitate to a colourless one. Lead stays insoluble. Aluminium, zinc and lead, and their oxides and hydroxides, react with both acids and alkalis, so they are amphoteric.

notes.title: Analytical Chemistry — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Colours of salts and their solutions
sections.body_md:
**Qualitative analysis** identifies the ions in a substance from observations such as colour and precipitates.

- **White solids, colourless solutions:** salts of Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺, NH₄⁺, Zn²⁺ and Pb²⁺.
- **Copper(II):** hydrated CuSO₄ blue crystals, blue solution; CuCl₂ green to blue-green; CuO black; CuCO₃ green.
- **Iron(II):** FeSO₄·7H₂O pale green crystals, pale green solution.
- **Iron(III):** FeCl₃ yellowish-brown solid and solution; Fe₂O₃ reddish brown.
- **Zinc and lead oxides:** ZnO white (yellow when hot); PbO yellow; Pb₃O₄ bright red; PbO₂ dark brown.

key_terms.definition_md: Finding out which ions or substances are present, without measuring how much.
An insoluble solid that forms when two solutions are mixed.

sections.heading: 2. Sodium hydroxide: coloured precipitates
sections.body_md:
Sodium hydroxide supplies OH⁻ ions; insoluble metal hydroxides precipitate. Add it **drop by drop**, then **in excess**.

- **Fe²⁺:** dirty green Fe(OH)₂, insoluble in excess (turns brown on standing in air: oxidised to Fe(OH)₃).
- **Fe³⁺:** reddish-brown Fe(OH)₃, insoluble in excess.
- **Cu²⁺:** pale blue Cu(OH)₂, insoluble in excess.
- **Ca²⁺:** white Ca(OH)₂ (sparingly soluble), insoluble in excess.

key_terms.definition_md: Adding a reagent a little at a time so that the first change can be seen before an excess is present.

visual.alt: Table of precipitates formed by sodium hydroxide with four cations and their behaviour in excess

sections.heading: 3. Sodium hydroxide: zinc and lead
sections.body_md:
Zinc and lead salts give **white** precipitates that **dissolve in excess** NaOH, because their hydroxides are amphoteric.

- **Zn²⁺:** white gelatinous Zn(OH)₂ → dissolves to **sodium zincate**, Na₂ZnO₂ (colourless solution).
- **Pb²⁺:** white chalky Pb(OH)₂ → dissolves to **sodium plumbite**, Na₂PbO₂ (colourless solution).

key_terms.definition_md: Na₂ZnO₂, the soluble salt formed when zinc, its oxide or its hydroxide reacts with sodium hydroxide.
Na₂PbO₂, the soluble salt formed when lead, lead(II) oxide or lead(II) hydroxide reacts with sodium hydroxide.

visual.alt: Table of zinc and lead ions with a little and excess sodium hydroxide

sections.heading: 4. Ammonium hydroxide, a few drops and in excess
sections.body_md:
A few drops of NH₄OH give the **same precipitates** as NaOH (an ammonium salt stays in solution). In **excess**:

- **Cu(OH)₂ dissolves** → **deep (inky) blue** solution of tetraamminecopper(II) sulphate, [Cu(NH₃)₄]SO₄.
- **Zn(OH)₂ dissolves** → **colourless** solution of tetraamminezinc(II) sulphate, [Zn(NH₃)₄]SO₄.
- **Pb(OH)₂, Fe(OH)₂, Fe(OH)₃ do not dissolve.**

Plain-text equation for copper in excess: Cu(OH)₂ + (NH₄)₂SO₄ + 2NH₄OH → [Cu(NH₃)₄]SO₄ + 4H₂O (zinc follows the same pattern).

key_terms.definition_md: A solution of ammonia in water; a weak alkali.
The deep blue soluble complex salt formed when copper(II) hydroxide dissolves in excess ammonium hydroxide.

visual.alt: Table comparing the behaviour of five cations in excess sodium hydroxide and excess ammonium hydroxide

sections.heading: 5. Sodium hydroxide and ammonium salts
sections.body_md:
Any **ammonium salt warmed with an alkali** gives **ammonia**: the stronger base drives out the weaker one.

**Identifying ammonia:** pungent smell; turns **moist red litmus blue**; gives **dense white fumes** of NH₄Cl with a rod dipped in concentrated HCl (NH₃ + HCl → NH₄Cl).

key_terms.definition_md: Warm the substance with sodium hydroxide solution: ammonia is given off, which turns moist red litmus paper blue.

visual.alt: Table of three tests that identify ammonia

sections.heading: 6. Amphoteric nature of aluminium, zinc and lead
sections.body_md:
**Amphoteric:** reacts with **both acids and bases** to form a salt and water. Examples: Al₂O₃, ZnO, PbO and Al(OH)₃, Zn(OH)₂, Pb(OH)₂.

- **Metals with hot concentrated NaOH** give **hydrogen**: aluminium (with water) → sodium aluminate; zinc → sodium zincate; lead → sodium plumbite.
- **Oxides and hydroxides with NaOH** give the same salts and **water** (no hydrogen).
- With KOH the products are potassium aluminate, zincate and plumbite.

key_terms.definition_md: A substance that reacts with both acids and bases to form a salt and water.
NaAlO₂, the soluble salt formed when aluminium, its oxide or its hydroxide reacts with sodium hydroxide.

visual.alt: Table of the products when aluminium, zinc, lead and their oxides or hydroxides react with sodium hydroxide

| Fe²⁺ / Fe³⁺ | NaOH | dirty green / reddish brown |
| Zn²⁺ / Pb²⁺ | excess NH₄OH | precipitate dissolves / stays |

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Swapping the colours of Fe(OH)₂ (dirty green) and Fe(OH)₃ (reddish brown).
- Saying Cu(OH)₂ dissolves in excess NaOH (it dissolves in excess NH₄OH).
- Using excess NaOH to tell zinc from lead (it dissolves both).
- Leaving water out of the aluminium–NaOH equation.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Observation questions (1 mark each): colour **and** behaviour in excess where asked.
- Equations (1 mark): correct formulae and balancing; name the salt (zincate, plumbite, aluminate) if asked.
- Distinguish questions (2 marks): one reagent, one observation for each substance.

answer.model_answer_md:

questions.stem_md:
Five solutions, A to E, each contain one of the cations Fe²⁺, Fe³⁺, Cu²⁺, Zn²⁺ and Pb²⁺. The observations are:

- A: colourless; a white precipitate with sodium hydroxide that dissolves in excess; a white precipitate with ammonium hydroxide that does not dissolve in excess.
- B: blue; a pale blue precipitate with sodium hydroxide that does not dissolve in excess.
- C: yellowish brown; a reddish-brown precipitate with sodium hydroxide.
- D: colourless; a white precipitate that dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide and also in excess ammonium hydroxide.
- E: pale green; a dirty green precipitate with sodium hydroxide.

(a) Identify the cations in B, C and E. [3]

(b) Identify the cations in A and D, and explain how the test with ammonium hydroxide decides between them. [3]

(c) (i) What would be seen if ammonium hydroxide were added to B until in excess? (ii) Taking D to be zinc sulphate, write the balanced equations for its reaction with a little sodium hydroxide and with excess sodium hydroxide. (iii) The precipitate from E is left to stand in air for a day. What change is seen, and why? [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) B: Cu²⁺. C: Fe³⁺. E: Fe²⁺.

(b) A: Pb²⁺. D: Zn²⁺. Both hydroxides are white and amphoteric, so both dissolve in excess sodium hydroxide; but only zinc hydroxide dissolves in excess ammonium hydroxide (forming a soluble complex), so the solution whose precipitate dissolves is zinc and the one whose precipitate stays is lead.

(c) (i) A pale blue precipitate forms, which dissolves in excess to give a deep (inky) blue solution. (ii) ZnSO₄ + 2NaOH → Zn(OH)₂ + Na₂SO₄; Zn(OH)₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂ZnO₂ + 2H₂O. (iii) The dirty green precipitate turns reddish brown, because iron(II) hydroxide is oxidised by the air to iron(III) hydroxide.
